message.content:
The sea appears most often as **blue**—but its hue actually depends on several factors:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **Water molecules & Rayleigh scattering** | Short‑wavelength (blue) light scatters more than longer wavelengths, giving clear water a natural blue tint. |
| **Depth** | Deeper water absorbs red/orange/green wavelengths; only blue survives, so deeper parts look darker or even indigo. |
| **Surface conditions** | Calm surfaces reflect sky colors; windy seas scatter sunlight differently, sometimes producing turquoise or greenish tones. |
| **Algae / phytoplankton** | High concentrations give a greenish or brownish appearance due to chlorophyll absorption. |
| **Sediment / turbidity** | Suspended particles can make water appear murky, gray, or reddish if iron oxides dominate. |
| **Sun angle & time of day** | Morning/evening sun casts warmer hues (golden, pink), while midday gives clearer blues. |

So while “the sea” is commonly described as blue, it’s really a spectrum influenced by depth, composition, weather, and lighting.
